title: 5. Leading Operational KPIs, Structural Potential & CEO Walk-the-Talk

epigraph.quote: Our digital vision at Costco is to deliver a seamless experience that builds trust and loyalty with our members, both in warehouse and online.
epigraph.author: Ron Vachris, President & CEO, Costco Wholesale (Q1 FY2026 Earnings Call)

web_blocks.html: Costco caps its retail margins by design. As a result, gross-margin expansion does not measure business health. Five leading operational KPIs tell the real story instead [6, 7]. Analysts must track adjusted comparable sales, paid member growth, Executive penetration, renewal rates, and new warehouse productivity [6, 7].

In FY2026, total comparable sales rose 8.4%, or 6.6% excluding gas and foreign exchange [7]. Adjusted comps grew 6.6% in the U.S., 6.7% in Canada, and 6.5% in Other International [7]. Paid members climbed 3.8% YoY to 84.1 million, lifting total cardholders to 150.4 million [6]. Paid Executive members jumped 9.4% to 42.3 million [6, 16]. That tier crossed 50% for the first time at 50.3% of paid members and drove 75.2% of net sales [6, 16]. Digitally-enabled comparable sales surged 20.9% (20.7% ex-gas/FX) to top $33 billion for the year [7, 16]. Triple-digit growth in personalization and sub-one-hour delivery via Instacart, Uber Eats, and DoorDash powered that gain [7, 16].

One nuanced KPI watchpoint deserves close scrutiny: renewal rates. U.S. and Canada renewal held flat at 92.3% in FY2026, while worldwide renewal held at 89.8% [6]. Both sit slightly below the FY2024 peaks of 92.9% in U.S./Canada and 90.5% worldwide [6]. Management tied this ~60–70 bps plateau to online promotional sign-ups and younger member cohorts [6, 16]. Members under 40 now exceed 25% of the base, up nearly 60% since COVID [6, 16]. These younger members renew at lower rates and spend less in year one before maturing into bigger spenders [6, 16].

web_blocks.caption: Costco 6-Year Leading Operational KPI Dashboard (FY2021–FY2026)
web_blocks.takeaway: Executive upgrades are up 65% since FY2021 to 42.3M, and Costco added 124 warehouses in five years. Together, they compound fee income at an ~8.8% CAGR, even as renewals sit ~60–70 bps off FY2024 highs.

web_blocks.title: 5.2 Structural Growth Runway & Physical Expansion Cadence

web_blocks.html: Costco's structural growth runway rests on three clear pillars. First, management is pushing net new openings toward a 30+ annual run rate [16, 20]. FY2027 plans call for 33 gross openings, 28 net new boxes, and 5 relocations [16, 20]. Planned FY2027 capex rises to ~$7.5 billion from $6.44 billion in FY2026 to fund that buildout [16, 20]. Second, international white space remains wide open across Europe, China, Canada, and Mexico [13, 20]. Costco runs just 11 continental European warehouses across Spain, France, and Sweden, plus 7 in China [13, 20]. FY2027 includes 4 European, 5 Canadian, and 1 Mexican opening, plus new U.S. cities like Buffalo, New York and Lawrence, Kansas [13, 20]. Third, digital personalization and retail media are scaling fast [9, 16]. Personalized items already appear in 10% of Costco.com orders, while AI pharmacy tools drove mid-teen script growth in FY2026 [9, 16].

We ran a 4-year audit of management's public promises from FY2022 through FY2026 [8, 9, 16, 27]. It spans Craig Jelinek (through Dec 2023), CEO Ron Vachris (since Jan 2024), and CFO Gary Millerchip (since March 2024) [8, 9, 16, 27]. The team earned high say-do marks across fee restraint, store growth, digital upgrades, and cash returns [8, 9, 16, 27].

web_blocks.title: 5.4 Capital Allocation Priorities, Executive Upgrade Funnel & Labor-Productivity Equation

web_blocks.html: Under Ron Vachris and Gary Millerchip, capital allocation stays strictly organic and owner-friendly [9, 16, 20]. First priority goes to high-return warehouse openings, backed by ~$7.5 billion in FY2027 capex [6, 20]. Management targets 33 gross and 28 net new boxes with over 80% land-and-building ownership [6, 20]. Recent FY2025 openings averaged $192 million in Year-1 sales [6, 20]. Second priority funds cold-chain depots, Costco Logistics hubs, and digital AI tools [9, 16]. Third priority supports steady regular dividend growth [7, 27]. Costco ended FY2026 with $21.3 billion in cash and short-term investments [7, 27]. Rather than chasing M&A, the board returns surplus cash via special dividends: $15/share in January 2024 and $30/share (~$13.3 billion) in November 2026 [7, 27].

Two operational levers drive medium-term earnings power: the Executive upgrade funnel and the wage-productivity equation [6, 24]. The Executive card costs $130 per year and pays a 2% reward capped at $1,250 [6, 15]. A household breaks even on the $65 upgrade fee at $3,250 in annual spend [6, 15]. Cashiers prompt Gold Star members at checkout once trailing spend clears that hurdle [6, 15]. That prompt helped lift Executive penetration to 50.3% of paid members and 75.2% of net sales [6, 15]. Meanwhile, Costco's March 2025 wage deal raised average U.S. hourly pay to ~$31–$32/hour, with $1.00/hour top-of-scale step-ups through 2027 [4, 6, 24]. Those wages support ~94% first-year retention and low shrink [4, 6, 24]. As a result, $317 million+ sales per warehouse easily absorb wage inflation inside ~9.15% SG&A [4, 6, 24].

book_paragraphs: If you want to know whether Costco is still firing on all cylinders without ever glancing at a stock chart, there are five numbers you should check every quarter: adjusted comparable sales, paid member count, Executive penetration, renewal rates, and Year-1 sales at newly opened warehouses. In FY2026, four of those five flashed bright green, while one flashed a gentle amber that any disciplined analyst should respect.

Let's start with the green lights. Comparable sales excluding gasoline inflation and foreign exchange grew 6.6% globally in FY2026—a remarkable pace for a $300 billion retailer. Paid members grew 3.8% to 84.1 million households (150.4 million total cardholders), and Executive members surged 9.4% to 42.3 million. Think about that milestone: for the first time, more than half of Costco's paying members (50.3%) are on the $130 Executive tier, and those Executive households account for 75.2% of worldwide net sales. Meanwhile, digitally-enabled sales topped $33 billion, growing nearly 21%.

book_subsections.title: The Renewal Watchpoint & CEO Walk-the-Talk Audit
paragraphs: Now look at the amber light: renewal rates. In the U.S. and Canada, renewal held steady at 92.3% in FY2026, and worldwide renewal ticked up 10 basis points sequentially to 89.8%. Those are still world-class retention numbers, yet they sit 60 to 70 basis points below the FY2024 peak of 92.9% and 90.5%. Why? Because Costco has been attracting a wave of younger members under 40—now over a quarter of the base, up nearly 60% since COVID—and signing up more members via online promotions, which historically renew at slightly lower rates in year one before maturing as household size and income grow.

That is why the CEO Walk-the-Talk audit under Ron Vachris and CFO Gary Millerchip is so reassuring. Rather than chasing short-term margin optics, management reinvested part of its Q4 FY2026 IEEPA tariff refunds directly into lower member prices, expanded sub-one-hour delivery across Instacart, Uber Eats, and DoorDash, and committed ~$7.5 billion in FY2027 capex to open up to 33 warehouses (28 net new, 5 relocations) across both new U.S. cities like Buffalo and Lawrence and international markets in Europe, Canada, and Mexico. And when cash still piled past $21.3 billion on the August 2026 balance sheet, the board didn't go shopping for an unrelated acquisition—it declared a $30-per-share special dividend in November 2026, returning roughly $13.3 billion straight to owners.

book_subsections.title: How Vachris and Millerchip Allocate Every Dollar of Cash
paragraphs: When a business generates $15,825 million in operating cash flow and holds $21.3 billion in cash and short-term investments, the biggest risk isn't running out of money—it's management doing something foolish with the surplus. Look at how Ron Vachris and Gary Millerchip rank every dollar of capital. First in line is organic warehouse growth: Costco is stepping up capital spending to roughly $7.5 billion in FY2027 to open up to 33 gross warehouses (28 net new, plus 5 relocations), buying the land and building outright whenever possible because new boxes are now averaging $192 million in Year-1 sales.

Second in line is infrastructure that widens the moat—cross-docking depots, Costco Logistics capacity, Digital Wallet checkout tech, and AI pharmacy inventory tools. Third is the regular quarterly dividend. And when cash still piles up after funding every high-return project on the board, management doesn't hunt for an expensive unrelated acquisition to look busy. Instead, the board writes a massive special dividend check straight to owners—$15 per share in January 2024, followed by $30 per share (roughly $13.3 billion) in November 2026.

book_subsections.title: The Executive Upgrade Funnel and the Wage-Productivity Bargain
paragraphs: Behind those cash flows sit two quiet operational flywheels that you should understand as a business analyst. The first is the Executive Membership upgrade funnel. A Gold Star card costs $65, and an Executive card costs $130—a $65 step-up that pays you 2% back on qualified purchases up to $1,250 a year. Do the math: once your household spends $3,250 a year at Costco, that 2% rebate pays the entire $65 upgrade difference. Costco's register systems track when a Gold Star shopper crosses that spend pace and prompt the cashier to offer an upgrade right at checkout. That simple math is why Executive members grew 9.4% in FY2026 to 42.3 million households—now 50.3% of paid members driving 75.2% of total sales.

The second flywheel is Costco's wage-productivity bargain. Paying U.S. hourly employees an average of ~$31 to $32 an hour—with $1.00-per-hour top-of-scale increases locked in every March from 2025 through 2027—looks expensive on a spreadsheet if you only look at hourly rates. But because turnover sits near 8% and first-year retention hovers near 94%, Costco's forklift drivers, meat cutters, and cashiers know the floor cold, move pallets faster, and keep inventory shrink a fraction of the retail average. High wages don't hurt Costco's $317 million-per-warehouse productivity; they are one of the main reasons it exists.

Ultimately, that combination of $7.5 billion in organic warehouse capex, a $3,250 Executive upgrade funnel, $31-to-$32 hourly wages, and a $30-per-share special dividend tells you everything you need to know about Issaquah's culture. Management is not trying to outsmart Wall Street with financial engineering; it is simply reinvesting into the box, sharing scale with members and employees, and handing the leftover cash straight back to shareholders.

book_callouts.title: What to Watch on Renewal Rates
book_callouts.text: If U.S./Canada renewal drifts below 91.5% over the next four quarters, it would signal that digital promotional sign-ups or fee-hike elasticity are diluting cohort quality. Conversely, if under-40 members mature into Executive upgrades as they form households, renewal should stabilize above 92%.

book_callouts.title: Special Dividends as Capital-Allocation Honesty
book_callouts.text: When a mature compounder declares a $30-per-share special dividend (~$13.3 billion) rather than chasing flashy M&A, it is telling you two things: management respects its circle of competence, and the core warehouse model produces far more cash than it can prudently reinvest.
